prompt.context: Our client, Giant Bank, is one of the 'big 4' banks in Australia. These 4 banks account for about 75% of the retail/commercial banking revenue in Australia and are roughly equal in size. Giant Bank does not have a good understanding of the profitability of its retail customer base, and more specifically individual segments. One segment that has been of particular concern to them is the 'youth' customer segment. This group encompasses all customers under the age of 22.
prompt.question: Giant Bank wants Bain to help answer two questions: (1) What is the average annual profit of a Youth customer? (2) What should Giant Bank's strategy be to maximize long-term profits for this customer segment?

clarifying_info.q: What are the revenue sources for a youth customer?
clarifying_info.a: Revenue comes from two sources: interest revenue and fee revenue. Exhibits with detailed data are available upon request.

clarifying_info.q: What costs are associated with serving a youth customer?
clarifying_info.a: Costs include channel costs (branch, ATM, internet, phone) and product-related costs. Exhibits with detailed breakdowns are available upon request.

clarifying_info.q: How does the youth segment compare to other segments in terms of products owned?
clarifying_info.a: The youth segment owns significantly fewer products than other segments (except for the Community segment). Exhibit data shows product ownership by segment.

clarifying_info.q: Are the costs to serve youth customers primarily fixed or variable?
clarifying_info.a: The bulk of costs are fixed. Youth customers are negative profit but likely positive contribution given the fixed cost structure.

exhibits.title: Revenue and Cost Data by Customer Segment
exhibits.shows: Charts showing revenue (interest and fee) and cost breakdown for the youth customer segment and comparisons to other segments
exhibits.data: Interest revenue, fee revenue, channel costs, and product ownership data by segment — specific figures available in exhibit images not captured in text extraction

framework: Define profitability = Revenue minus Costs for the youth segment
Revenue breakdown: Interest revenue (from deposits and loans) + Fee revenue (transaction fees, account fees)
Cost breakdown: Channel costs (branch visits most expensive, internet cheapest) + Product servicing costs
Calculate average annual profit per youth customer = Total revenue per customer minus Total cost per customer
Assess strategic options to improve long-term profitability of the youth segment

questions.prompt: Q1: What is the average annual profit of a Youth customer? Walk through your calculation approach.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure as Profit = Revenue - Costs. Revenue = interest revenue + fee revenue. Costs = channel costs (branch being most expensive, internet being cheapest at <$0.01 fully costed) + product costs. The answer requires using the exhibit data. A strong candidate proactively asks for the exhibits and organizes the calculation cleanly. The final answer (per the interviewer note on p85) comes from the exhibit data — youth customers are unprofitable on a fully-allocated basis but likely positive on a contribution basis since most costs are fixed.

math.setup: Profit per youth customer = (Interest revenue + Fee revenue) - (Channel costs + Product costs)
steps: Identify interest revenue per youth customer from Exhibit data
Identify fee revenue per youth customer from Exhibit data
Identify channel costs: branch costs are 10x-100x more expensive than internet (internet < $0.01 fully costed)
Sum total costs per youth customer
Net profit = Total revenue - Total costs
math.answer: Youth customers are net unprofitable on a fully-allocated basis (exact figure requires exhibit image data not captured in text extraction)

questions.prompt: Q2: What strategy should Giant Bank pursue to maximize long-term profits from the youth segment?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates should consider both short-term profit improvement (fees, channel migration) and long-term value (future profitability as youth customers age). Should distinguish between actions that are clearly good, those with potential, and those to avoid. Key insight: youth customers are negative profit but positive contribution — so mass attrition is bad. Another key insight: these customers are the future profitable customers of the bank.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic options does Giant Bank have to improve the profitability of its youth customer segment?

categories.name: Raise or Introduce Fees
ideas: Increase revenue from the youth segment directly
If done correctly, can influence behavior positively — e.g., reduce branch visits by charging for branch transactions
Must be careful not to lose too many customers since youth are negative profit but positive contribution
Fees should be in line with market or likely to be followed by the other 3 banks to avoid competitive disadvantage

categories.name: Redirect Customers to Cheaper Channels
ideas: Branch costs are 10x-100x more expensive than cheaper channels
Internet transactions can cost less than $0.01 fully costed
Use positive reinforcement: education, easy secure login for internet banking
Use negative reinforcement: fees for expensive channels like branch transactions
Many customers will migrate to cheaper channels with the right mix of incentives

categories.name: Shut Down Unprofitable Branches (Has Potential)
ideas: Bulk of cost reduction will ultimately come from branch rationalization
However, unlikely that any branch serves predominantly youth customers — cross-segment analysis needed first
Requires a full footprint analysis quantifying profitability, contribution, and customer segments served by branch

categories.name: Aggressively Cross-Sell Other Products (Has Potential)
ideas: Youth segment owns significantly fewer products than other segments (except Community)
Credit cards are a high-potential cross-sell product
However, youth customers may genuinely not need other banking products yet
Cross-selling in financial services has historically shown disappointing results — further analysis required before recommending

categories.name: Targeted Marketing to Acquire More Youth Customers (Use Caution)
ideas: Giant Bank should NOT broadly acquire more unprofitable youth customers
Exception: selectively target older youth (21-22 year old college graduates) who are likely to become profitable soon
Timing is critical — acquiring too young means years of losses with no guarantee of retention when the customer becomes profitable

recommendation: Giant Bank's youth segment is currently unprofitable on a fully-allocated basis but likely positive on a contribution basis
In the short term, Giant Bank should raise or introduce fees (in line with market) and redirect youth customers to cheaper channels (especially internet banking) to reduce costs
In the medium term, conduct a full branch footprint analysis to identify branches that can be rationalized across all segments
In the long term, selectively target older youth customers (21-22 year old graduates) who represent future profitable customers, while avoiding broad youth acquisition spending
risks: Raising fees too aggressively could cause customer attrition — lost customers mean lost future profitable relationships
Competitors may not follow fee increases, putting Giant Bank at a competitive disadvantage
Youth customers who leave may switch to a competitor and become profitable customers there
Branch closures require cross-segment analysis and may alienate other profitable customer groups
next_steps: Conduct channel cost analysis and model the savings from shifting youth transactions from branch to internet
Analyze fee sensitivity and competitive benchmarking to determine optimal fee structure
Run full branch footprint analysis across all customer segments
Model lifetime value of youth customers as they age into more profitable segments
